speaker: Doctor
text: I see you have a history of ataxia; to better understand your condition, could you tell me when you first noticed your gait instability and if it has been progressive or sudden? Additionally, have you experienced any numbness, weakness, or changes in your vision recently?

speaker: Patient
text: I started having trouble walking recently, and people say I look drunk when I walk. I also feel clumsy in my arms and legs, especially on the right side.

speaker: Doctor
text: That sounds concerning; given the "drunk" appearance and right-sided clumsiness, have you noticed any double vision, slurred speech, or difficulty swallowing? Also, have you had any recent headaches or loss of balance while standing still, not just when walking?

speaker: Patient
text: I have Crohn disease and it has been difficult to control. I have been taking natalizumab for about a year.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for that crucial information; since you are on natalizumab for Crohn's disease, we must urgently rule out Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML). Can you tell me if you have noticed any recent changes in your memory, personality, or muscle weakness specifically in your hands? REQUEST TEST: MRI Brain with contrast.

Also, please describe the exact nature of your double vision if you have it, and whether it improves by closing one eye. REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Brain axial and coronal views.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRI Brain Findings: Lesions consistent with Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy (PML). T1/T2 images showing multifocal demyelinating lesions without gadolinium enhancement, indicative of PML.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) secondary to natalizumab therapy.

Please confirm that you have no new onset of fever or altered mental status, as we must immediately stop natalizumab and consider starting highly active antiretroviral therapy or other immunomodulators if a co-infection is suspected. We will also arrange a consultation with neurology to monitor the progression of the lesions.
